chief_complaint: high fever, septic pulmonary emboli with cavitary lung lesions, and right-sided heart murmur
hpi_details: 33M active IV methamphetamine user presenting with bacteremia, bilateral nodular cavitary lung infiltrates, and TEE showing 2 cm vegetation on tricuspid valve requiring repair/replacement.
ideas: He thinks he caught a severe chest infection or pneumonia from using a contaminated needle or bad street dope.
concerns: He is worried that being admitted to the hospital will cause severe drug withdrawals and cost him his construction job.
expectations: He hopes to receive strong intravenous antibiotics right away to clear the fever so he can be discharged today.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Tricuspid Valve Endocarditis (IV drug use) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Tricuspid Valve Endocarditis (IV drug use) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management requires prolonged IV antibiotics targeted to blood culture results (empiric coverage for Staphylococcus aureus, the most common organism in IVDU-associated tricuspid endocarditis) and surgical evaluation when there is persistent bacteremia, recurrent septic emboli, or right heart failure.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: high fever, septic pulmonary emboli with cavitary lung lesions, and right-sided heart murmur

Key HPI features: 33M active IV methamphetamine user presenting with bacteremia, bilateral nodular cavitary lung infiltrates, and TEE showing 2 cm vegetation on tricuspid valve requiring repair/replacement.
Objective/Exam findings: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Tricuspid Valve Endocarditis IV Drug Use.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Tricuspid Valve Endocarditis (IV drug use).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Left-sided (aortic/mitral) endocarditis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Respiratory distress with new cavitary lesions — signals ongoing septic embolization.
management_principles: Start empiric IV antibiotics (e.g., vancomycin) after blood cultures are drawn, then narrow therapy once the causative organism and sensitivities are known
Consult cardiothoracic surgery and infectious disease; counsel on harm-reduction and substance-use treatment referral
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.assessment: Findings consistent with tricuspid valve infective endocarditis complicated by septic pulmonary emboli, in the context of injection drug use.
reference_soap.plan: Draw blood cultures x2-3 sets before starting antibiotics; begin empiric IV vancomycin pending sensitivities; obtain TTE/TEE; consult cardiothoracic surgery and infectious disease; counsel on harm-reduction and substance-use treatment referral.

teaching.one_liner: Bacteria introduced through injection drug use seed the tricuspid valve, and vegetation fragments embolize to the lungs, causing septic pulmonary emboli with cavitary lesions and fever.
red_flags: Respiratory distress with new cavitary lesions — signals ongoing septic embolization

must_ask.say: Can you tell me about your drug use — what and how often you inject?
How long have you had fevers?
Any cough, chest pain, or coughing up blood?
Have you had any skin infections at your injection sites?
Have you had a heart valve infection before?

history.answer: I came in because I've had a burning high fever and violent shaking chills for the past four days that just won't go away.
The fever started out of nowhere four days ago and has stayed consistently severe day and night.
My thermometer at home read up to 39.2 degrees, and I keep having severe shivering fits where my whole body shakes.
I took acetaminophen 500 mg yesterday, but my fever barely dropped for an hour before spiking right back up.
I've had a dry cough and mild chest tightness, and I get winded more easily when walking, but no sore throat or runny nose.
I have not had any burning when I urinate, no need to pee more often, and no lower back or flank pain.
My stomach feels fine, and I haven't had any nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
I don't have a severe headache, my neck bends without stiffness, and my mind feels totally clear.
I haven't noticed any skin rashes, dark insect bite scabs, or joint swelling and pain.
I have been waking up drenched in sweat every night, but I haven't noticed any noticeable weight loss over the past few weeks.
I haven't felt any swollen lumps or tender glands in my neck, armpits, or groin.
I haven't traveled outside the country recently, spent time in the woods, or had contact with animals.
No one at home or around me has been sick with a fever or any infection.
I have never received chemotherapy, and I do not take steroid pills or any immune-suppressing drugs.
I have never had artificial heart valves or known heart murmurs, and I haven't had any dental cleanings or procedures done recently.
I haven't started taking any new medications, herbs, or over-the-counter supplements lately.
I haven't had any new sexual partners, but I do inject methamphetamine into my arm veins several times a week.
My left inner arm where I inject had some redness and soreness last week, though the redness has faded slightly.
I have never had a heart valve infection or been treated for endocarditis before.
I figured I must have picked up a nasty chest bug or pneumonia from a dirty needle I used a few days back.
I'm really terrified that getting stuck in a hospital bed is going to trigger horrible withdrawals and get me fired from my job.
I was really hoping you could just give me a strong dose of IV antibiotics to knock out this fever so I can head home today.
I have a history of high blood pressure and mild high cholesterol, but nothing else.
I had an uncomplicated appendectomy when I was seventeen, with no other surgeries or hospital admissions.
I take lisinopril 10 mg once daily every morning for my blood pressure.
I don't have any known allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I don't smoke tobacco cigarettes and I don't use vape products.
I only drink one or two beers on the weekend, nothing heavy.
I work remotely as a freelance graphic designer and live alone in an apartment.
My father has high blood pressure, but there is no family history of heart valve disease or early heart failure.

exam.finding: Patient appears acutely ill, diaphoretic, and fatigued, but is alert and conversational.
Blood pressure is 118/74 mmHg, pulse 112 beats per minute, respirations 22 breaths per minute, temperature 39.1°C, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air.
Oropharynx is clear without erythema, petechiae, or tonsillar exudate.
Both tympanic membranes are clear, pearly gray, and intact bilaterally.
No palpable anterior or posterior cervical lymphadenopathy.
Scattered bilateral inspiratory crackles at both lung bases without audible wheezing.
Grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur heard best along the lower left sternal border that intensifies during inspiration, with regular tachycardia and no gallop.
Abdomen is soft, non-distended, and non-tender without guarding or rebound tenderness.
No hepatomegaly or splenomegaly palpable below the costal margins.
No costovertebral angle tenderness on percussion bilaterally.
Visible needle track marks in the left antecubital fossa with mild localized tenderness, but no fluctuant abscess, Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, or splinter hemorrhages.
Supple neck with full active flexion and negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs.
